items.title: [Editorial] Climate change and health: 10 years on, what next?

items.title: [Comment] Offline: China bids to lead in global health

But from the perspective of an emerging superpower, it was not surprising at all. The Chinese Government is ready to assert its claim to positions of global leadership, especially now that the USA has turned its back on multilateralism. In Beijing last week, I sat down with Dr Li to listen to her set out her manifesto. She has four pillars supporting her pitch: a more efficient WHO; a safer world; equitable health systems; and harnessing innovation.

items.title: [Correspondence] Women with obstetric fistula in Somalia deserve better

The profiles are a useful description of sensory heterogeneity. However, the disease-duration analysis does not show that they represent successive stages of CRPS.

items.title: Sugammadex versus neostigmine for reversal of neuromuscular blockade and postoperative pulmonary complications: reversal adequacy in the SNaPP pragmatic trial
items.summary: We read with interest the Sugammadex, Neostigmine and Postoperative Pulmonary Complications (SNaPP) trial by Leslie and colleagues,1 which reported that sugammadex reduced the incidence of postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) compared with neostigmine in adults aged 40 yr or older undergoing abdominal or thoracic surgery. As a pragmatic trial, SNaPP provides valuable evidence about real-world reversal practice, but interpretation depends critically on whether the observed benefit reflects the reversal agent itself or the adequacy of neuromuscular recovery before extubation.

items.title: Silencing the fire alarm: responding to intraoperative blood pressure targets
items.summary: A meta-analysis in a recent issue of the British Journal of Anaesthesia pools randomised evidence on intraoperative arterial blood pressure targets in nine trials in noncardiac surgery. With a total of 14 658 patients included in the analysis, the authors show that higher mean arterial pressure targets do not reduce 30-day mortality, acute kidney injury, or myocardial injury. These findings reinforce the distinction between low blood pressure as a marker of perioperative vulnerability and low blood pressure as a modifiable therapeutic target.
